verdict: OK to lend in Bhadohi carpets — back the hand-made exporter with order proof and tight monthly stock-and-receivable discipline; skip the leveraged trader with no order book.
title: Bhadohi Carpets & Rugs: a note to the credit manager
narrative:
## What this business physically is
**Bhadohi hand-makes carpets and rugs, and the local trade says the district makes India's largest share of hand-made carpet [1].** The unit buys yarn and dyes, pays weavers per knot or per square foot, and sells finished rugs to exporters and overseas buyers. Cash sits in loom-stage work-in-progress and in finished stock waiting for a container, not in the building. **So when a proposal lands, check the weaver payment cycle and the finished-goods holding days first; if stock days exceed the order-to-shipment window, ask why.**

## Where value and cash sit
**Pricing power is thin at the loom and thick at the buyer's brand, so margin lives in design, colourways and repeat orders.** The working-capital cycle is the whole credit: yarn and wages go out early, export receivables come back late. **Take the export receivable ageing and the buyer-wise order book every month; if one buyer crosses a third of sales, ask for the buyer's payment history.** Capex is modest — looms, dyeing, maybe a finishing line — so term debt should stay small and short. ## What has changed now
**The official data pack reads OK at 76, with Uttar Pradesh GST collections up 14.2% Apr-to-date against India's 6.1% [D] — a real local tailwind.** India-wide carpet-relevant output (NIC 13) is up 13.1% YoY [D]. **But the local sources are thin: the Bhadohi coverage we have is a general trade piece [1] and topic pages [2][3], so lean on first principles and peers for the rest.** Peer results are mixed — Faze Three grew revenue 32.92% to ₹932.76 crore in FY26 while operating profit fell 20.15% [5]; Welspun Living targets double-digit UK growth and low double-digit flooring margins [6]. **So when a proposal lands, check whether volume growth is reaching the bottom line; if sales are up but margin is flat, ask for the price list and the yarn cost sheet.**

## Who to pursue, who to avoid
**Pursue the hand-made exporter with repeat overseas buyers, own dyeing, and a clean receivable record; pursue the small weaver-cooperative aggregator with verified order confirmations.** **Avoid the pure trader with no loom base and high working-capital utilisation — a peer rating showed limits around 80% utilised for twelve months with cash of 0.22 crore [10].** Rating reports flag inventory management as the key sensitivity [8] and note weaving is fixed- and working-capital intensive [11]. ## How to grow safely
**Structure as a cash-flow loan against confirmed export orders, with a stock-and-receivables charge and a monthly stock statement.** Covenant on buyer concentration and receivable days. **Take monthly: stock statement, export invoice register, weaver wage payout proof, and GST returns.**

## Early warning signs
**Watch stretched limit utilisation, rising finished-stock days, and a single buyer delaying payment.** Any of these means stop enhancement and re-price.
watch: finished-stock days rise beyond the order-to-shipment window -> ask for the buyer order and hold fresh limits
turnover falls while limits stay drawn -> freeze enhancement and review the drawing power
one buyer crosses a third of sales -> ask for that buyer's payment history and diversify covenant
